[exc_dd1e65de648fb2_998_v1] Learning Statistics with R — Statistical tools › 15 Linear regression › 15.2 Estimating a linear regression model › 15.2.1 Using the lm() function (pages 610)
roles: formal | topics: using-r, anova, linear-regression, center, estimation
synopsis: The lm() function is a fairly complicated one: if you type ?lm, the help files will reveal that there are a lot of arguments that you can specify, and most of them won’t make a lot of sense to you. At this stage however, there’s really only two of them that you care about, and as it turns out you’ve seen them before:

• formula. A formula that specifies the regression model. For the simple linear regression models that we’ve talked about so far, in which you have a single predictor variable as well as an intercept term, this formula is of the form outcome ~ predictor. However, more complicated formulas are allowed, and we’ll discuss them later.
• data. The data frame containing the variables.

As we saw with aov() in Comparing several means (one-way ANOVA), the output of the lm() function is a fairly complicated object, with quite a lot of technical information buried under the hood. Because this technical information is used by other functions, it’s generally a good idea to create a variable that stores the results of your regression. With this in mind, to run my linear regression, the command I want to use is this:

regression_1 <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood

)

As we saw with aov() in Comparing several means (one-way ANOVA), the output of the lm() function is a fairly complicated object, with quite a lot of technical information buried under the hood. Because this technical information is used by other functions, it’s generally a good idea to create a variable that stores the results of your regression. With this in mind, to run my linear regression, the command I want to use is this:

regression_1 <- lm( formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood

)

Note that I used danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep as the formula: in the model that I’m trying to estimate, danielle_grump is the outcome variable, and danielle_sleep is the predictor variable. It’s always a good idea to remember which one is which! Anyway, what this does is create an “lm object” (i.e., a variable whose class is "lm") called regression_1. Let’s have a look at what happens when we print() it out:

print(regression_1)

Call: lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)

Coefficients:

(Intercept) danielle_sleep 125.956 -8.937

title: Simple Linear Regression in R with lm()
content:
# Simple Linear Regression in R with `lm()`

## 1. Fitting the model

`lm()` takes two key arguments:

- **`formula`** — the model, written as `outcome ~ predictor` (outcome on the left, predictor on the right).
- **`data`** — the data frame containing the variables.

```r
regression_1 <- lm(formula = danielle_grump ~ danielle_sleep, data = parenthood)
```

The result is an "lm object" holding lots of technical information, so store it in a variable. Printing it shows the model call and the coefficients:

```r
print(regression_1)
# Coefficients:
# (Intercept)  danielle_sleep
#     125.956          -8.937
```

## 2. The fitted line

The printed coefficients give the best-fitting regression line:

$$\hat{Y}_i = -8.94\,X_i + 125.96$$

## 3. Interpreting the coefficients

- **Slope ($\hat{b}_1$ = −8.94):** for each 1-unit increase in the predictor, the outcome changes by the slope. Here, each additional hour of sleep reduces grumpiness by 8.94 points.
- **Intercept ($\hat{b}_0$ = 125.96):** the expected value of the outcome when the predictor equals 0. Here, zero hours of sleep predicts a grumpiness score of 125.96. (Interpret it cautiously if X = 0 is outside the observed data range.)

## 4. Getting the full picture: `summary()`

```r
summary(regression_1)
```

The summary output contains, line by line:

- **Call** — the model you fit.
- **Residuals** — a five-number summary of the errors (Min, 1Q, Median, 3Q, Max).
- **Coefficients table** — for each coefficient: `Estimate`, `Std. Error`, `t value`, `Pr(>|t|)` (p-value), plus significance stars (`***` p < 0.001, `**` p < 0.01, `*` p < 0.05, `.` p < 0.1).
- **Residual standard error** — typical size of the prediction error, with degrees of freedom.
- **Multiple / Adjusted R-squared** — proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the model (e.g. R² = 0.816 means ~82% of the variation is explained).
- **F-statistic** — overall test of whether the model fits better than an intercept-only model, with its p-value.

## 5. Quick workflow

```r
model <- lm(y ~ x, data = mydata)   # fit
summary(model)                      # coefficients, p-values, R²
plot(mydata$x, mydata$y)            # scatterplot
abline(model, col = "red")          # add the fitted line
hist(model$residuals)               # check residual distribution
plot(mydata$x, model$residuals)     # residual plot vs. predictor
abline(h = 0)
```

---

*Sources: Learning Statistics with R (Ch. 15, Linear regression); Advanced High School Statistics (§5.3.5, R commands for regression).*

resource.title: Simple Linear Regression in R with lm()

answer:
Created the study note **Simple Linear Regression in R with lm()** — a concise, single-note walkthrough covering:

- **Fitting** the model with `lm(formula = outcome ~ predictor, data = ...)` and storing the lm object
- **The fitted line** from printed coefficients (worked example: grumpiness ~ sleep, Ŷ = −8.94X + 125.96)
- **Interpreting** the slope (change in outcome per unit of predictor) and intercept (expected outcome at X = 0, with a caution about extrapolation)
- **Reading `summary()` output**: residuals, coefficient table with estimates, standard errors, t values, p-values and significance stars, residual standard error, R², and the F-statistic
- **A quick workflow** snippet with plotting (`plot`, `abline`) and residual checks (`hist(model$residuals)`, residual plot)

Built from *Learning Statistics with R* (Ch. 15) with R-command details from *Advanced High School Statistics* (§5.3.5).
